title: California signs first US AI audit laws — AB 1405 stands up an auditor registry, SB 813 certifies verification bodies
subtitle: Governor Newsom signed a two-bill package that puts a state licensing regime around independent AI audits, with the first certified verification organizations due by January 2028 and the auditor registry going live in 2029.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: California Governor Gavin Newsom signed Assembly Bill 1405 and Senate Bill 813 on September 9, 2026, creating the first US legal framework that requires third-party audits of high-risk AI systems and licenses the auditors that perform them. AB 1405, from Assemblymember Rebecca Bauer-Kahan, sets up a state registry for AI auditors with independence rules modeled on the accounting profession — beginning in 2029, no covered AI audit in California can be performed by anyone who is not on the registry. SB 813, from state Senator Jerry McNerney, gives the California Government Operations Agency until January 1, 2028 to certify the first class of Independent Verification Organizations that will actually assess models and systems for compliance with state law.

The mechanism matters more than the headline. Both bills together look like a licensing regime for the audit market, not just a mandate to be audited — the state decides who is qualified to test frontier models and hiring tools, publishes the list, and can revoke registration for independence violations. That is the same structural move the SEC made for public-company auditors after Sarbanes-Oxley, and it is the first US instance of that move applied to AI. Anthropic and OpenAI both publicly backed the package, which is notable because the industry has resisted almost every state-level AI bill so far; the read is that a state-run auditor registry is preferable to the alternative of individual states writing their own conformance tests one by one.

The scope reaches beyond frontier labs. AB 1405 sweeps in employment-decision AI, consumer-facing generative systems above defined thresholds, and any covered developer doing business in California — which given the state's economic weight, functionally means most vendors. The two-year on-ramp is deliberate: it gives the Government Operations Agency time to set independence standards, gives auditors time to build practices, and gives developers time to instrument their systems for the kinds of tests IVOs are expected to run. It also lines up with the EU AI Office's high-risk audit rollout, which we covered on September 6 — a US state and the EU converging on the same regulatory shape within days of each other is the story here.

Takeaway for learners: this is the first time an AI-audit role has a licensed profession attached to it, and that means the job is now a real career track — not a research hobby. If you are early in your career and interested in AI safety or governance, the credentialing path being built right now is the one you can enter through: audit methodology, model documentation, evaluation design, and independence discipline. The next two years will decide who staffs those firms. Watch the Government Operations Agency's rulemakings; they will tell you what the qualifying skills actually are.
